subject: storytime
title: The Tale of Two Bad Mice
about: Beatrix Potter's 1904 tale of Tom Thumb and Hunca Munca, two mice who creep into a doll's house while the dolls are out, find that the lovely dinner is plaster, and make a glorious mess, then feel sorry and make it right with a crooked sixpence and a broom. First graders love the hard-as-a-rock ham and the chair going down the mouse hole. It is a public-domain book retold here in first-grade words, five pages long; the real one with Potter's pictures is at the library.
tip: Ask him what he would do if his dinner turned out to be plaster, then find the two ways the mice said sorry.

book.author: Beatrix Potter (retold)
book.source: public domain, retold in first-grade words
book.blurb: Two mice, a doll's house, and a dinner made of plaster.

passage.text:
Once there was a lovely doll's house.
It had red brick walls and white windows.
Two dolls lived there, Lucinda and Jane.
Jane was the cook.
But she never cooked a thing.
The dinner came in a box, all ready made.
There was a ham, two fish, and a pudding.
It all looked so yummy.
***
One morning, the dolls went out for a ride.
The house was very quiet.
Two little mice peeked out of a hole.
They were Tom Thumb and Hunca Munca.
They crept into the doll's house.
"Look at the dinner!" said Tom Thumb.
"Yum!" said Hunca Munca.
***
Tom Thumb tried to cut the ham.
His knife bent.
The ham was hard as a rock.
It was not real food at all.
It was made of plaster!
The fish was plaster.
The pudding was plaster, too.
Tom Thumb was so cross.
He dropped the ham on the floor.
Crack! It broke in two.
***
Then the two mice made a big mess.
They pulled the feathers out of the pillows.
They pulled the clothes out of the drawers.
They pushed a chair down their mouse hole.
They took the cradle, too.
Then the dolls came home.
Lucinda and Jane just stared.
What a mess!
***
That night, the mice felt sorry.
Tom Thumb found a crooked sixpence under the rug.
It was a little bent coin.
He left it for the dolls.
"That will pay for the ham," he said.
And Hunca Munca?
Every morning, very early, she comes with her broom.
She sweeps the doll's house clean.
Sweep, sweep, sweep!

cards.q: Who lived in the doll's house?
cards.note: The two dolls live there; the mice only crept in from their hole while the dolls were out.

cards.q: What was the dolls' dinner really made of?
cards.note: The ham was hard as a rock and the knife bent: ham, fish and pudding were all plaster.

cards.q: What did the mice push down their mouse hole?
cards.note: They also took the cradle and pulled the feathers out of the pillows and the clothes out of the drawers.

cards.q: What did Tom Thumb leave to pay for the ham?
cards.note: A sixpence is an old coin; this one was bent, and he found it under the rug.

cards.q: What happened first in the story?
cards.note: The dolls go out for a ride, the house is quiet, and only then do the mice peek out of their hole.

cards.q: What happened at the end of the story?
cards.note: Every morning, very early, she comes with her broom and sweeps the doll's house clean.

cards.q: How did the mice feel that night?
cards.note: They felt sorry for the mess, so Tom Thumb paid for the ham and Hunca Munca sweeps the house.

cards.q: Where did the two mice find the dinner?
cards.note: The setting is where a story happens: a doll's house with red brick walls and white windows.

cards.q: In the story, what does 'crooked' mean?
cards.note: A crooked sixpence is a bent coin, not straight and flat like a new one.

cards.q: Which word is in the story?
cards.note: He reads the three words himself; only one of them is in the story.
